newsitem.title: GERMANY: German parliament passes multimedia law.
newsitem.headline: German parliament passes multimedia law.

text.p: German parliament on Friday passed legislation that sets the framework for government regulation of the Internet and sets the stage for the development of new multimedia services in business and entertainment.
The law sets standards for child protection in cyberspace and defines which activities require regulation and which can be operated without any formal license or regulatory oversight.

It distinguishes between traditional media forms that use the Internet, and should therefore fall under media rules, and new services, such as electronic mail or video conferencing, that the government says should not be classified as media.
The Information and Communications Services Act, set to take effect on August 1, is one of the first pieces of law that outlines a legal framework for the wilds of the Internet.
"With this law we are taking on a vanguard position," said Justice Minister Edzard Schmidt-Jorzig. "Germany desparately needs to grasp its opportunities this time."

The law was passed in the lower house of parliament with the majority of the ruling centre-right coalition government. It must still pass in the upper house, which is controlled by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) before it can take effect. The upper house will vote on the bill on July 4.

The legislation also provides a framework for law enforcement officials, who have been uncertain about who should be held responsible for the publication of illegal material on the Internet such as extremist writings and child pornography.

Authorities in Bavarian state recently indicted the former head of the German unit of online service CompuServe for dissemination of child pornography, sparking sharp protests from industry and civil rights advocates.

The new law would make such online service providers responsible for illegal material accessible over their networks only "if they are aware of the material and it would be technically possible and reasonable" to block access to such material.
The Federation of German Industry (BDI) welcomed passage of the bill as a first step towards providing a secure framework for investment in new media and information services.
But opposition politicians said the government's bill would hinder investment and damage the trust of ordinary citizens in the new technologies.
